Chapter 4: Global Solidarity—Building Bridges Beyond Borders.
You know, there’s a moment in every struggle when the world feels impossibly huge… and yet, somehow, deeply connected. Maybe you’ve seen it yourself—a protest in one city sparks demonstrations halfway across the globe. Messages of support travel over oceans, through social media, handwritten letters, or even whispered prayers. Suddenly, that feeling of isolation starts to fade. Why? Because you realize you’re not alone. Others are out there, fighting for dignity and justice too.
Solidarity—now, that’s more than just a word or a slogan. It’s a practice, a way of looking at the world that refuses to accept the lines drawn by states or empires. Remember when people in Ferguson got advice from activists in Palestine about dealing with tear gas? It’s a powerful reminder: The tools of repression might be shared, but so are the tools of resistance.
Of course, these connections aren’t always obvious. Picture a student in London learning about the Black Panther Party, and suddenly seeing the same echoes in their own city’s fight against police violence. Or imagine a worker in South Africa, finding inspiration in the civil rights movement in the US. The details might shift from place to place, but the heart of it—the demand for freedom, for dignity, for the right to live without fear—well, that stays the same.
Building bridges across borders isn’t easy. It takes a lot of humility and a real willingness to listen and learn. It’s about understanding that no one struggle is more important than another, and that everyone has something to teach—and something to learn. It also means facing up to the ways privilege and power shape our world, even within movements that are supposed to be about justice.
For many of us, the first step is just paying attention. Maybe a parent reading the news notices the same words used to describe protesters in different countries. Or a teacher encourages students to look beyond their neighborhood, to see how local and global struggles connect. These small acts—curiosity, care—they add up. Little by little, they weave a web of solidarity that’s stronger than any wall.
The work of building global solidarity never really ends. It happens in meetings, in marches, and even in those quiet moments when you’re just thinking things through. It takes patience, persistence, and sometimes, the courage to be uncomfortable. But it brings something beautiful too—a sense that you’re part of something bigger, sharing hope and determination with people all over the world.
Most people don’t realize just how much power lives in these connections. When movements learn from each other, they grow more creative, more resilient, and better able to challenge the systems that hold them back. The lessons of one struggle often become the seeds for another, carried across borders by the winds of hope.
